tasks.q: What does a denial-of-service attack set out to do?
a: Stop real users from being able to use a service
Steal passwords from a database
Encrypt files for a ransom
Read data as it crosses the network
tasks.fb: It denies service: that's exactly what the name says.

tasks.q: What is the main cost of a DoS attack to a business?
a: Downtime: lost sales and customers while the service is unavailable
The electricity used by the attack
The cost of new keyboards
Nothing, if no data is stolen
tasks.fb: An online shop that's offline earns nothing.

a: A network of infected computers controlled by an attacker
A program that blocks adverts
A type of firewall
A backup server
tasks.fb: Each infected machine is called a zombie.

tasks.q: Why is a distributed attack harder to stop?
a: The traffic comes from thousands of different addresses, so it's hard to tell it from real users
It uses less bandwidth
It only happens at night
It comes from one address that is easy to block
tasks.fb: Blocking one address does nothing when there are 100,000 of them.

tasks.q: What were most of the devices in the Mirai botnet?
a: Internet-connected devices such as cameras and routers, still using default passwords
Supercomputers in universities
Games consoles owned by the attacker
Company mail servers
tasks.fb: Smart devices are rarely updated and often ship with the same password.

tasks.q: Why did attacking a DNS provider knock out so many sites?
a: Without DNS, browsers couldn't turn domain names into IP addresses
It deleted the websites
It encrypted every web page
It switched off the undersea cables
tasks.fb: The sites were still running; nobody could find them.

tasks.q: Which are effects of a successful DDoS attack on a company? Select all that apply.
opts: Customers can't buy anything while the site is down
Staff unable to use internal systems
The company's data is automatically encrypted
correct: Customers can't buy anything while the site is down
Staff unable to use internal systems
tasks.fb: A DoS attack doesn't steal or encrypt data: it blocks access.

tasks.q: Why might attackers launch a DDoS as a distraction?
a: The security team is busy, so another attack may go unnoticed
It backs up the data first
It switches off the firewall by law
It makes the servers faster

tasks.q: How does rate limiting help against a DoS attack?
a: It caps how many requests each source can make, so floods are throttled
It encrypts the web pages
It hides the server's IP address forever
It deletes the attacker's account
tasks.fb: Genuine users rarely make hundreds of requests a second.

tasks.q: Which helps stop your devices being used in a botnet?
a: Changing default passwords and keeping devices updated
Turning the router upside down
Using a longer network cable
Paying the ransom
tasks.fb: Mirai spread entirely through default passwords.

tasks.q: Why does knowing normal traffic patterns help?
a: Because an unusual spike stands out as a possible attack
Because attacks only happen on Mondays
Because it makes servers faster
Because it encrypts the traffic
tasks.fb: Detection is the first step in responding.

tasks.q: Paying a website to 'stress test' someone else's server is:
a: Illegal under the Computer Misuse Act
Fine if you don't do it yourself
Legal if the attack fails
Legal if you are under 18
tasks.fb: People have been prosecuted in the UK for using these services.

stations.name: Final challenge: the anatomy of a DDoS

tasks.q: Put the stages of a DDoS attack in order.
steps: Malware infects thousands of poorly secured devices
The infected devices become zombies in a botnet
The attacker sends a command to the botnet
Every zombie sends requests to the target server at once
The server runs out of capacity and stops responding to real users
tasks.fb: This is the illustration you need for your Hacker's Handbook page on denial of service.

info.title: It's not always an attack
info.text: A sudden rush of genuine visitors, such as tickets going on sale, can knock a site over too. That's sometimes called the 'hug of death'.

info.title: Mirai's source code
info.text: The code behind the Mirai botnet was published online, so copies of it are still scanning the internet for weak devices today.

info.title: Attack sizes
info.text: The largest recorded DDoS attacks have exceeded the capacity of entire countries' internet connections, measured in terabits per second.

info.title: Smart devices
info.text: Your fridge, doorbell or camera can join a botnet. Change default passwords and install updates on anything you connect to the internet.

info.title: Absorbing floods
info.text: Large providers protect customers by spreading traffic across many data centres, so no single server has to take the whole flood.

info.title: Ransom DDoS
info.text: Some criminals threaten a DDoS attack unless a company pays. Police advise reporting it and not paying.
